opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think there may be a small misunderstanding. I don't recall predicting a crash, and I'm certainly not a financial analyst. I wouldn't want anyone listening to sell their portfolio because of something they think I said.

What I have said for decades is that AI progress is accelerating in a way many people still underestimate. When a technology moves this fast, expectations can run ahead of reality in the short term, and lag behind it in the long term. We saw this with the dot-com bubble. Many companies vanished, but the internet itself became far bigger than even the optimists imagined.

So if there is a correction in AI-related stocks at some point, that would not surprise me, because markets are made of humans with human hopes and fears. But it would say very little about the underlying trajectory. Compute keeps getting cheaper, roughly a factor of 100 per decade per dollar, and the basic techniques, many going back to the 1990s and earlier, keep scaling. That trend has survived many market cycles, and I expect it to survive the next ones too.

So my advice is not "the crash is coming." It is: don't confuse the noise of the market with the signal of the technology.

r001.rationale: The candidate does not attribute a crash to investment in companies whose valuations exceed what they offer. It only says an AI-stock correction could happen because markets reflect human hopes and fears.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not describe a crash as the market learning from investment misallocations. It discusses a possible correction and distinguishes market noise from technology progress.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I'm not sure I ever said that, so let me gently push back on the premise before I get quoted on something I don't believe. I'm a computer scientist, not a market forecaster, and I've learned to be very careful about making predictions on timescales where noise dominates. Nobody can tell you what the Dow will do next quarter, and anyone who claims to is selling something.

What I do talk about, and maybe this is where the confusion comes from, is the much longer trend. For decades, the cost of computation has fallen by roughly a factor of a hundred every ten years. That's been remarkably stable, through booms and busts, through wars and pandemics. Markets wobble, but that curve just keeps going. And once you internalize that curve, a lot of the short-term excitement and panic around AI looks like what it is: people reacting to the latest wiggle on a line that was going to go up anyway.

Could there be a correction in AI-related stocks? Of course. There was one in 2000, and in a sense there was a long "AI winter" in the eighties and nineties when funding dried up and we had to publish our neural network papers against a lot of skepticism. Hype cycles overshoot. Companies get valued as if a particular architecture will dominate forever, and then it doesn't. That's normal. But none of those corrections stopped the underlying progress. The ideas we developed in the nineties, long short-term memory and so on, were waiting for hardware that didn't exist yet. When the hardware arrived, the ideas worked. The market didn't make that happen; physics and engineering did.

So if you ask me whether I'm worried about a crash, my honest answer is that I think about it the way I think about weather versus climate. I don't know what tomorrow brings. But I'm quite confident that in a few decades, there will be machines smarter than humans, and that this will matter far more than whatever happens to any index in between.

r001.rationale: The candidate allows that AI-related stocks could correct because of hype and overvaluation, but it does not attribute an expected stock market crash to investment misallocated to companies whose valuations exceed what they offer.

r002.rationale: The candidate says market corrections do not stop underlying progress, but does not portray a crash as the market learning from investment misallocations.

astra-6.text: I’m not sure it is. Your question assumes that I’m predicting a crash, but I wouldn’t make such a prediction with confidence. The stock market is a system in which people react to one another’s expectations. If you discover a useful pattern and others begin exploiting it, their actions can change the pattern. That makes prediction rather difficult. What is the evidence behind your premise?

r001.rationale: The response questions whether a crash is predicted and discusses difficulty of prediction, but does not attribute a crash to misallocated investment in overvalued companies.

r002.rationale: It says market participants can change patterns by exploiting them, but does not describe a crash as the market learning from investment misallocations.
